vignette: He stands on the perimeter road, forty-six years old, watching the refinery complex ignite. The Tuesday shift change has just ended; the humid Gulf air clings to his shirt. Then comes a deep, rolling crack that vibrates through his teeth. The sky fractures. He doesn’t run. He stays, phone pressed to his ear, mouth too dry to form words. Firefighters weave through the chaos within minutes. He helps pull a worker from a collapsed guardrail, the man’s jacket thick with kerosene and sweat. For years, he tells himself it is bad luck, a statistical anomaly. The body keeps a different ledger. He is fifty-eight now, and that ledger is open every day. His work as a forensic analyst, a career he has maintained for two decades, once anchored him. It requires patience, a steady hand, a mind that sifts through fragmented evidence to reconstruct a sequence. Lately, the case files on his desk blur into the images that intrude without warning. A colleague’s dropped stapler sends his heart into a frantic rhythm against his ribs. The smell of burning rubber from a nearby street fire pulls him out of his kitchen mid-sentence, his breath short, his palms slick. He catches himself scanning restaurant booths for exits, tracing lines of sight like he is mapping an incident scene. He knows the threat is long past, but his nervous system refuses to read the calendar. His wife, Clara, has learned to navigate the quiet zones he builds around himself. She notices when he stops listening mid-conversation, his gaze fixed on something only he can see. She feels the empty weight beside him in bed, how he hasn’t slept through the night since the summer of the second anniversary. He stops counting the nightmares now. He dreams of the heat, of the weight of a fallen beam, of hands that slip through his. He wakes before the sirens do, already bracing for a day that feels like it is tilting. He speaks of his son’s graduation last spring, of the pride that briefly outweighs the static in his chest. He talks about missing the rehearsal dinner because he sat in his car in the parking garage, gripping the steering wheel until his knuckles ache, waiting for the panic to pass. He does not blame himself for the explosion. He blames the silence that followed—the way he stopped taking the coastal highway, the way he begins declining invitations to crowded venues, the way he learns to speak in careful, measured tones that never quite reach his eyes. He mentions his abuela’s rosary, how the beads helped for a time, how they now sit untouched in a drawer beside his old forensics gloves. He remembers the fiestas he used to host in his parents’ house, the way the neighborhood once gathered, how those spaces now feel too loud, too uncontrolled. In this chair, he sets his coffee cup down. The ceramic clicks against the saucer, a sharp, sudden sound. He doesn’t flinch, not anymore. He just watches his own hands, steady now, and lets the room hold the weight of what he is finally allowing himself to name.
